title: Qualifier Review: Comprehensive Problem Solving
subject: Qualifier
summary: Problem-solving workshops in qualifying-exam style: strategy and estimation, then mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, thermal and statistical physics, and mixed problems, with two full mock qualifying exams.

units.title: Strategy and estimation
units.summary: Problem-solving habits that win qualifying exams: dimensional analysis, limiting cases, order-of-magnitude estimates, and the constants worth memorizing.

lessons.title: Dimensional Analysis and Limiting-Case Checks
objectives: Apply dimensional analysis (Buckingham Pi) to predict the functional form of a result up to a dimensionless constant, and use it to check a derived answer.
Check any final formula against at least three limits (zero, infinity, symmetric case) and against units before moving on.

lectures.title: Lecture 1: Powers of Ten - Units - Dimensions - Measurements - Uncertainties - Dimensional Analysis - Scaling Arguments

demoIdeas: Dimensional-analysis drill: given a physical situation and its variables, find the dimensionless groups and test candidate formulas for dimensional consistency.
Limit-checker: type a candidate formula for a block sliding on an incline and see it plotted against the free-fall and theta -> 0 limits with sliders for h and theta.

lessons.title: Exam Strategy: Triage, Time Budget and Written Plans
objectives: Triage a six-problem exam: select the problems to attempt, budget time per problem, and decide when to stop and move on.
State assumptions and a plan in the first lines of each solution so partial credit is available.
demoIdeas: Exam time-budget planner: set your confidence and the point value for each of six problems, drag the time allocation, and see the expected score and the best triage order.

lessons.title: Atomic and Thermal Energy Scales
objectives: Estimate atomic scales from first principles: Bohr radius, Rydberg energy 13.6 eV, fine-structure constant, and thermal energy k_B T of about 1/40 eV at room temperature.
Use hc of about 1240 eV nm to move between wavelength, photon energy, and temperature; connect to bond energies and spectroscopic regions familiar from chemistry.

lectures.title: Lecture 1: Powers of Ten - Units - Dimensions - Measurements - Uncertainties - Dimensional Analysis - Scaling Arguments

demoIdeas: Energy-scale ladder: a log-scale ruler marking k_BT, rotational, vibrational, bond, Rydberg and keV-MeV scales; drag a temperature or wavelength marker to see which type of transition it can drive.

lessons.title: Fermi Estimates and Error Budgets
objectives: Estimate the number of molecules in a room, the power radiated by a human body, or the energy stored in a thunderstorm to within an order of magnitude.
State the uncertainty of an estimate and identify the dominant source of error.

lectures.source: Univ. of Canterbury Faculty of Engineering (Dr Phil Wilson)
lectures.title: Fermi Problems: from toilet paper to housing the world

demoIdeas: Fermi-problem trainer: random estimation questions with a log-scale slider answer and feedback on the order-of-magnitude error, plus a tornado chart of which input dominates your uncertainty.

units.title: Mechanics workshops
units.summary: Qualifier-style problems from Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, central forces, non-inertial frames, oscillators, and special relativity.

lessons.title: Generalised Coordinates, Lagrangians and Constraint Forces
objectives: Choose generalized coordinates for a constrained system and write the Lagrangian for a pendulum on a moving support or a bead on a rotating hoop.
Find constraint forces using Lagrange multipliers.

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Lagrange Multipliers. Near Equilibrium Dynamics. Oscillators. (Lagrange multipliers and constraints)

demoIdeas: Block on a sphere: drag the starting offset and see the normal force plotted against angle, with the leave-off point where N reaches zero.

lessons.title: Equilibria, Small Oscillations, Normal Modes and Cyclic Coordinates
objectives: Find equilibrium points, assess stability, and compute small-oscillation frequencies and normal modes for coupled systems.
Use cyclic coordinates and Noether-type conservation laws to reduce the number of equations.

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Lagrange Multipliers. Near Equilibrium Dynamics. Oscillators. (near-equilibrium dynamics and oscillators)
Lecture 15: Systems with Many Degrees of Freedom. Normal Modes.

demoIdeas: Bead on a rotating hoop: slide the hoop's angular speed Omega and watch the effective potential develop two new equilibria beyond sqrt(g/R), with a normal-mode animation for coupled masses and springs.

lessons.title: Central Forces: Effective Potential, Kepler Orbits and Precession
objectives: Use the effective potential to classify orbits and test the stability of circular orbits in a central potential.
Solve Kepler problems with conserved energy, angular momentum, and the Runge-Lenz vector, and find precession caused by a small perturbation.

lectures.title: Lecture 8: Solution of the Two Body Problem.

demoIdeas: Orbit sandbox: choose potential (1/r, 1/r^3, r^2), energy and angular momentum; plot V_eff with the energy line and the resulting orbit, showing precession when a 1/r^3 perturbation is added.

lessons.title: Scattering, Rotating Frames and Rigid-Body Rotation
objectives: Compute collision kinematics in the lab and center-of-mass frames and the Rutherford scattering cross section.
Analyze motion in rotating frames (Coriolis and centrifugal forces) and torque-free rigid-body rotation using the inertia tensor.

lectures.title: Lecture 10: Rotating Reference Frames. Centrifugal, Coriolis and Euler Forces.
Lecture 12: Motion of Rigid Bodies. Inertia Tensor.

demoIdeas: Scattering sandbox: shoot particles at a central potential and watch deflection angle versus impact parameter and the resulting cross section.

Rotating-frame viewer: throw a ball on a turntable and compare its straight path in the inertial frame with the curved path in the rotating frame; spin a book or racket about its three axes to see the intermediate-axis flip.

lessons.title: Hamiltonian Mechanics, Poisson Brackets and Adiabatic Invariants
objectives: Write Hamilton's equations, use Poisson brackets, and identify conserved quantities and phase-space flows (Liouville's theorem).
Apply adiabatic invariants to slowly varying systems.
keyEquations: \dot q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p},\ \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}
\{f,g\}=\sum_i\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q_i}\right)
demoIdeas: Phase-space flow: draw a blob of initial conditions and evolve it under a free particle, a harmonic oscillator, a pendulum or a damped oscillator, with the area readout showing conservation except with damping.

lessons.title: Driven Oscillators and Relativistic Kinematics
objectives: Solve the driven damped oscillator, finding amplitude, phase, resonance width, and quality factor Q.
Solve relativistic decay and collision problems with four-momentum conservation, thresholds, and invariant masses.

lectures.title: Lecture 5: Harmonic Oscillator. Damped & Driven Oscillators. Greens Functions.

demoIdeas: Sliders for damping gamma and drive frequency omega; plot amplitude and phase versus omega and watch the resonance peak sharpen and the phase step sharpen as gamma goes to 0.

units.title: Electromagnetism workshops
units.summary: Qualifier-style problems: boundary-value problems, multipoles, induction, Poynting flow, waves in media, radiation, and relativistic transformations of fields.

lessons.title: Symmetry, Gauss's and Ampere's Laws, Multipoles and Energies
objectives: Use symmetry and Gauss's or Ampere's law for fields of spheres, cylinders, and planes.
Compute multipole moments and far-field potentials.
Compute energies of charge and current configurations.

lectures.source: Univ. of Rochester PHYS 415 (Teitel, Fall 2024), graduate-level
lectures.title: 1-2.2 Maxwell's equations for magnetostatics

demoIdeas: Multipole viewer: place point charges and see the monopole, dipole and quadrupole parts of the far-field potential, with a log-log plot of each term against distance.

lessons.title: Boundary-Value Problems and Fields in Matter
objectives: Solve Laplace's equation by images and by separation of variables in Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.
Handle dielectrics and magnetic materials with bound charges/currents and boundary conditions.

lectures.source: Univ. of Rochester PHYS 415 (Teitel, Fall 2024), graduate-level
lectures.title: 2-1.2 The Poisson equation as a boundary value problem, electrostatic boundary conditions

lectures.title: 2-3.3 Separation of variables in spherical coordinates

demoIdeas: Grounded sphere in a uniform field and a dielectric slab in a capacitor: sliders for permittivity, field and sphere radius show the field lines, induced surface charge and the image charge.

lessons.title: Induction, Eddy Currents and Poynting Energy Flow
objectives: Compute induced EMFs and inductances with Faraday's law, including motional EMF and eddy-current problems.
Use displacement current and the Poynting vector to track energy flow, including in a charging capacitor.

lectures.source: Univ. of Rochester PHYS 415 (Teitel, Fall 2024), graduate-level
lectures.title: 1-3.1 Faraday's Law, Maxwell's correction to Ampere's Law, waves, systems of units

lectures.title: 4-1.1 Electromagnetic energy and energy conservation

demoIdeas: Eddy-current brake: a magnet falls through a conducting tube; sliders for conductivity and magnet strength show the terminal velocity, with induced current loops drawn.
Poynting vector map around a charging capacitor and a resistor: arrows show energy flowing in from the sides while the current is steady.

lessons.title: Waves in Media: Reflection, Skin Depth, Plasmas and Waveguides
objectives: Solve reflection and transmission at a dielectric interface and the skin depth in a conductor.
Use the plasma frequency and dispersion relation for waves in plasmas and waveguide cutoff.

lectures.source: Univ. of Rochester PHYS 415 (Teitel, Fall 2024), graduate-level
lectures.title: 5-1.1 Electromagnetic waves in matter

lectures.source: Univ. of Rochester PHYS 415 (Teitel, Fall 2024), graduate-level
lectures.title: 5-5.3 Coefficient of reflection

demoIdeas: Wave at an interface: sliders for the two refractive indices and angle of incidence show reflected and transmitted waves, the Fresnel coefficients and Brewster's angle.
Plasma dispersion: plot omega versus k with the cutoff at the plasma frequency and show a wave entering a plasma being transmitted above cutoff and evanescent below.

lessons.title: Dipole Radiation, the Larmor Formula and Scattering
objectives: Compute dipole radiation patterns and power with the Larmor formula and estimate radiated power of an accelerating charge.
Estimate scattering by a bound electron in the Rayleigh and Thomson limits, including why the sky is blue.

demoIdeas: Dipole radiation pattern: animate a driven oscillating dipole with sliders for frequency and acceleration, plotting the sin^2(theta) angular pattern, the 1/r fall-off of the radiation field and the total Larmor power.

lessons.title: Retarded Potentials, Synchrotron Radiation and Field Transformations
objectives: Use retarded potentials and Lienard-Wiechert fields for moving charges and estimate synchrotron emission.
Transform E and B between frames and use the invariants E.B and E^2 - c^2 B^2.

lectures.source: Univ. of Rochester PHYS 415 (Teitel, Fall 2024), graduate-level
lectures.title: 7-2.4 Lorentz transformation of electric and magnetic fields

Synchrotron beaming: slider for gamma shows the emission cone narrowing to 1/gamma around the velocity of a circling charge and the gamma^4 power scaling.

units.title: Quantum mechanics workshops
units.summary: Qualifier-style problems: one-dimensional systems, operator methods, angular momentum and spin, perturbation theory, variational and WKB methods, and scattering.

lessons.title: One-Dimensional Bound States, Tunnelling and Parity
objectives: Find bound states and scattering coefficients for square wells, barriers, and delta potentials, including tunneling probabilities.
Apply parity and other symmetries to simplify problems.
demoIdeas: Finite-well and delta-well bound-state solver: sliders for depth and width show the energy levels, the wave functions, the number of bound states and the parity of each.

lessons.title: Ladder Operators, Wavepackets and Ehrenfest's Theorem
objectives: Use ladder operators for the harmonic oscillator to compute matrix elements, expectation values, and uncertainties.
Solve time evolution of wavepackets and use the Heisenberg picture and Ehrenfest's theorem.
demoIdeas: Coherent-state wavepacket in a harmonic well: its centre oscillates classically (Ehrenfest) while the width stays constant; overlay a wavepacket in an anharmonic well to see the centre deviate from the classical path.

lessons.title: Angular-Momentum Algebra and Addition
objectives: Use the angular-momentum algebra to find eigenvalues and matrix representations of L, J, and S.
Add angular momenta with Clebsch-Gordan coefficients (for example two spin-1/2 particles, or L + S).

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Spin One-half, Bras, Kets, and Operators

demoIdeas: Clebsch-Gordan coupler: pick j1 and j2 and see the coupled basis, the allowed J values and the coefficients as a table.

lessons.title: Spin in a Magnetic Field and Hydrogen Transitions
objectives: Solve spin-1/2 in a magnetic field: precession, Larmor frequency, and the connection to NMR.
Derive hydrogen energy levels with degeneracies and selection rules for electric dipole transitions.

lectures.title: Lecture 16: Quantum Dynamics (cont.) and Two State Systems

demoIdeas: Bloch-sphere trainer for spin-1/2 in a static plus rotating field (Rabi oscillations and NMR pulses).

lessons.title: Time-Independent Perturbation Theory and the Variational Method
objectives: Apply nondegenerate and degenerate time-independent perturbation theory (Stark effect, Zeeman effect, fine structure).
Use a trial wave function with the variational principle to bound a ground-state energy (helium, anharmonic oscillator).

lectures.title: L1.1 General problem. Non-degenerate perturbation theory
Lecture 24: Molecular Orbital Theory I. Variational Principle and Matrix Mechanics

demoIdeas: Anharmonic oscillator: a slider for the quartic coefficient lambda compares exact numerical energies with first- and second-order perturbation theory and a variational Gaussian trial function.

lessons.title: WKB, Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory and Scattering
objectives: Use WKB quantization and tunneling rates (Gamow factor).
Use first-order time-dependent perturbation theory and Fermi's golden rule, including sudden and adiabatic limits.
Compute scattering in the Born approximation and with low-energy partial waves.

lectures.title: L19.3 Differential and total cross section
L22.2 First Born Approximation. Calculation of the Scattering Amplitude

demoIdeas: Born amplitude explorer: choose a potential (Yukawa, Gaussian, square well) and see the Fourier-transform amplitude and dsigma/dOmega versus angle, with a WKB tunnelling-rate panel for the same barrier.

units.title: Thermal and statistical physics workshops
units.summary: Qualifier-style problems: thermodynamic potentials, partition functions (the chemist's home ground), quantum gases, and phase transitions.

lessons.title: Microcanonical Entropy, Maxwell Relations and Thermodynamic Potentials
objectives: Compute entropy and temperature from the microcanonical count for a paramagnet or Einstein solid.
Use Maxwell relations and thermodynamic potentials to derive response functions and heat-capacity relations.
demoIdeas: Two-state paramagnet: sliders for N and total energy show the number of microstates, S(E), and temperature from the slope, including the negative-temperature region.

lessons.title: Partition Functions, Heat Capacity and Thermodynamic Cycles
objectives: Compute the partition function for a two-level system, harmonic oscillator, and rigid rotor, and derive energy, entropy, and heat capacity (the Schottky anomaly).
Analyze engine and refrigerator cycles for efficiency, and ideal-gas processes including free expansion.
demoIdeas: Schottky anomaly: slider for the level splitting epsilon and a plot of mean energy and heat capacity versus temperature, plus a Carnot-cycle PV diagram with efficiency readout.

lessons.title: Degenerate Fermi Gases and Debye Solids
objectives: Compute the Fermi energy, pressure, and linear low-temperature heat capacity of a degenerate Fermi gas.
Apply the Debye model and obtain the T^3 low-temperature heat capacity.
demoIdeas: Fermi-Dirac occupation versus energy with a temperature slider and the Fermi sphere in k-space, alongside a Debye heat-capacity curve showing the T^3 rise and the Dulong-Petit plateau.

lessons.title: Bose Gases, the Photon Gas and Mean-Field Transitions
objectives: Compute the Bose-Einstein condensation temperature and the thermodynamics of a photon gas (Planck law, Stefan-Boltzmann).
Solve mean-field Ising and van der Waals models for critical temperatures and exponents.
demoIdeas: Condensate fraction N0/N = 1 - (T/Tc)^(3/2) versus T with a density slider, and a mean-field Ising magnetisation M(T) curve with a temperature slider showing the critical point.

units.title: Mixed problems
units.summary: Cross-topic problems typical of a qualifying exam, where atomic, solid-state, nuclear, and astrophysical scales mix mechanics, E&M, quantum mechanics, and statistical mechanics.

lessons.title: Hydrogen-Like Atoms and Nuclear Estimates
objectives: Scale hydrogenic results to positronium, muonic atoms, and hydrogen-like ions, and estimate Zeeman splittings and fine-structure sizes.
Estimate nuclear binding energy per nucleon, decay rates, and barrier penetration.

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Binding Energy, the Semi-Empirical Liquid Drop Nuclear Model, and Mass Parabolas

demoIdeas: Hydrogenic spectrum scaler: sliders for nuclear charge Z and the particle mass (electron, muon, positron) show the level diagram, the Bohr radius and transition wavelengths.

lessons.title: Free-Electron Metals, Semiconductors and Scaling Arguments
objectives: Use the free-electron model of a metal for conductivity, Hall effect, and Fermi velocity, and a band-gap argument for semiconductors.
Apply scaling arguments (Chandrasekhar-type or Debye-type) to find how a physical quantity depends on mass, charge, or temperature.
demoIdeas: Drude conductor: electrons drifting in an applied field with a scattering-time slider, Hall voltage readout, and resistivity versus temperature for a metal and an intrinsic semiconductor with a band-gap slider.

lessons.title: Choosing a Method and Spotting the Trick
objectives: Solve a problem that requires choosing among mechanics, E&M, quantum, and statistical methods without being told which.
Identify the 'trick' structure in a problem (symmetry, conserved quantity, dimensionless variable) before calculating.
demoIdeas: Mixed-problem randomizer drawing a timed problem from each course with a timer and a self-grading checklist.

lessons.title: Writing Complete Solutions and Diagnosing Weak Topics
objectives: Write a complete solution to a 30-minute problem in fewer than two pages with checks and limits.
Diagnose personal weak topics from the mock exams and build a one-page formula and method sheet.
demoIdeas: Weak-topic radar: enter your mock-exam scores by topic (mechanics, E&M, QM, stat mech, estimation) and see a radar plot, the biggest gaps and a suggested review order for the formula sheet.
